about: Phase 12 pilot: milestone events that open the Roman and Ottoman life-cycle phases (Ram, 2026-11-21: draft the missing ones).

events.name: Roman Empire Reaches Its Greatest Extent
aliases: Greatest extent of the Roman Empire
events.description: Under the emperor Trajan, conquests in Dacia and Mesopotamia bring the Roman Empire to its greatest size, stretching from Britain to the Persian Gulf. On Trajan's death his successor Hadrian gives up the new eastern provinces as too costly to hold.
events.note: The empire's extent peaked in 116–117; Trajan died in August 117 and Hadrian withdrew from Mesopotamia soon after.
events.significance: Trajan's conquests marked the high-water mark of Roman territory. Hadrian's decision to pull back and fortify the frontiers, as with his wall in Britain, shifted the empire from expansion to defence, a policy his successors largely kept.

events.name: Death of Marcus Aurelius
events.description: The emperor and Stoic philosopher Marcus Aurelius dies on campaign near the Danube frontier, and his son Commodus succeeds him. His death is often taken as the end of the long era of internal peace known as the Pax Romana.
events.note: Died 17 March 180, at Vindobona (Vienna) or Sirmium; sources differ. AT chosen for Vindobona.
events.significance: Marcus Aurelius was the last of a run of emperors chosen by adoption rather than birth. Passing power to his son Commodus, whose rule ended in assassination, opened decades of instability. His private Meditations became one of the most widely read works of Stoic philosophy.

events.name: Severus Alexander Murdered by His Own Troops
events.description: Soldiers on the Rhine frontier kill the emperor Severus Alexander and proclaim their commander, Maximinus Thrax. It opens about fifty years of civil wars, short reigns, invasions, plague and debased coinage, during which the empire briefly splits into three.
events.note: Killed in March 235 near Mogontiacum (Mainz). Name avoids 'Crisis of the Third Century' because it names the century.
events.significance: The murder began what historians call the Crisis of the Third Century, when some two dozen men claimed the throne in fifty years. The empire survived, but only after soldier-emperors such as Aurelian and Diocletian rebuilt its army and government.

events.name: Diocletian Becomes Roman Emperor
events.description: The army proclaims Diocletian, a soldier of humble birth from Dalmatia, as emperor. He ends the long run of short reigns, shares power with co-emperors in a tetrarchy of four rulers, and reorganises the provinces, taxes and army.
events.note: Proclaimed at Nicomedia (Izmit, Turkey) in November 284. The tetrarchy itself dates from 293; the description doesn't tie it to the accession year.
events.significance: Diocletian's reforms, a larger army, smaller provinces, a new tax system and power shared among several emperors, ended the crisis and set the pattern of the late Roman state. He is also remembered for the last great persecution of Christians.

events.name: Ottomans Capture Bursa
events.description: After a long siege, the forces of Orhan, son of the dynasty's founder Osman, take the Byzantine city of Bursa in northwest Anatolia. It becomes the first Ottoman capital and the burial place of the early sultans.
events.note: Bursa (Byzantine Prusa) fell in April 1326 after a siege of several years.
events.significance: Bursa gave the young Ottoman state a wealthy city, a capital and a base for further conquest. From there it expanded across northwest Anatolia and, within a generation, into the Balkans.

events.name: Ottomans Conquer Mamluk Egypt
events.description: Sultan Selim I defeats the Mamluk sultanate at Ridaniya outside Cairo and takes Egypt, having seized Syria the year before. The Ottomans gain the Nile's wealth and become the protectors of Mecca and Medina.
events.note: Ridaniya was fought in January 1517; Syria fell after Marj Dabiq (August 1516).
events.significance: The conquest made the Ottomans the leading power of the Islamic world: Egypt's grain and taxes enriched Istanbul, and guardianship of the holy cities gave the sultans new religious prestige. Ottoman rule in Egypt lasted, at least in name, until 1914.

events.name: Suleiman the Magnificent Becomes Sultan
events.description: Suleiman, the only surviving son of Selim I, succeeds his father. In a reign of forty-six years he takes Belgrade, Rhodes and much of Hungary, besieges Vienna, issues law codes that earn him the name Kanuni, the Lawgiver, and patronises the architect Sinan.
events.note: Acceded September 1520; died 1566 at the siege of Szigetvár.
events.significance: Suleiman's reign is often seen as the Ottoman high point: the empire reached deep into Europe, dominated the eastern Mediterranean and filled Istanbul with great mosques. Historians now stress that it stayed powerful long after him rather than declining from his death.

events.name: Ottoman Siege of Vienna Fails
events.description: A large Ottoman army under the grand vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieges the Habsburg capital, Vienna. A relief army led by the Polish king Jan III Sobieski routs the besiegers, and the defeat begins a long war in which the Ottomans lose Hungary.
events.note: The siege began in July; the relief battle was fought on 12 September 1683.
events.significance: The defeat at Vienna ended Ottoman expansion into central Europe. In the war that followed, a Holy League of the Habsburgs, Poland, Venice and later Russia took Hungary, the first large permanent loss of Ottoman territory in Europe.

events.name: Treaty of Karlowitz Signed
aliases: End of the Great Turkish War
events.description: After sixteen years of war with the Holy League, the Ottoman Empire makes peace at Karlowitz in Serbia, giving up most of Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs and other lands to Poland and Venice.
events.significance: Karlowitz was the first time the Ottomans formally gave up large European lands by treaty, and it marked a turn from expansion to defence on that frontier. The empire still won back ground later, including Belgrade, so it was not the start of a steady decline.

events.name: Selim III Becomes Sultan
events.description: Selim III comes to the throne in the middle of a losing war with Russia and Austria. He launches the New Order, a European-style army and new taxes to pay for it, but the Janissaries and their allies resist, and he is eventually deposed and killed.
events.note: Acceded April 1789; the New Order army dates from 1792–93; deposed 1807, killed 1808. The phase boundary is his accession (the source document's 1792 would be the army, not the reign).
events.significance: Selim III's New Order was the first systematic Ottoman attempt to remodel the state on European lines. It failed and cost him his life, but his successors Mahmud II and the Tanzimat reformers carried the same programme much further.

events.name: Edict of Gülhane Launches the Tanzimat Reforms
events.description: Under the young sultan Abdulmejid I, the government proclaims the Edict of Gülhane, promising security of life and property, fair taxation and regular military service for all subjects, Muslim and non-Muslim. It opens the period of reorganisation known as the Tanzimat.
events.significance: The Tanzimat modernised Ottoman law, schools and government and moved towards equal citizenship regardless of religion, leading to the first Ottoman constitution in 1876. It also met resistance at home and did not stop nationalist movements or European pressure.

events.name: Ottoman Empire Enters World War I
aliases: Ottoman entry into World War I
events.description: Allied with Germany, Ottoman warships bombard Russian ports on the Black Sea, and the empire enters the war against Russia, Britain and France. It goes on to fight at Gallipoli and in the Caucasus, Mesopotamia and Palestine.
events.note: Black Sea raid 29 October 1914; Russia, Britain and France declared war in early November.
events.significance: Entering the war proved fatal to the empire. Despite victories at Gallipoli and Kut it was defeated by 1918 and occupied, and the war years saw the Armenian genocide. The peace settlement divided its Arab lands between Britain and France, and the sultanate was abolished in 1922.
